text: Q4_K_M is 1.8x faster than MXFP4 on Apple Silicon. Tested Qwen3-14B at Q4_K_M and gpt-oss-20B at MXFP4 on the same M2 24GB Mac, same code-completion prompt, 3 trials each. Q4_K_M averaged 4.7 tok/s and finished a 200-token generation in 44 seconds. The MXFP4 model averaged 2.6 tok/s and took 71 seconds.

MXFP4 is a 4-bit microscaling floating-point format designed for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs and Apple's MLX backend. It has better numerical range than integer quants at the same bit count. On paper, MXFP4 should be faster on Apple Silicon because Apple has hardware support for microscaling FP in the M-series Neural Engine. In practice on M2, it is not faster than Q4_K_M.

Both models were loaded into Ollama before the timed trials. The first trial of each model is reported separately as a cold-load control; trials 2 and 3 are the warm-cache apples-to-apples comparison. The cold-load time is the Ollama-managed memory activation, not a disk read.

Tested 3 free LLM API providers and one paid Claude plan on the same 5 real coding tasks. All 20 runs passed on first attempt. OpenRouter Anthropic Haiku 4.5 averaged 2.9s wall time with 178 tok/s. Cline API Claude Opus 4.5 averaged 7.4s with 279 tok/s. Groq Qwen 3.6 27B averaged 8.8s with 511 tok/s. NVIDIA NIM Nemotron 120B averaged 27.0s with 409 tok/s.

The 3 free LLM API providers tested were NVIDIA NIM, Groq, and OpenRouter. Cerebras gpt-oss-120b and Z.ai glm-4-31b both returned 402 Payment Required when tested, so they were dropped from the comparison. Cline API turned out to be a paid Anthropic aggregator, not a free tier, but it was kept as a quality baseline against paid Claude.

One rate-limit hit on Groq (HTTP 429 on the refactor task), retried successfully and the retry was the one counted. No other rate limits or timeouts across 20 runs. The fastest single task was OpenRouter completing the file-deletion task in 1.4 seconds. The slowest was NVIDIA NIM at 47 seconds for the same task.

Speculative decoding on M2 24GB with Ollama 0.12.8, Qwen3 14B at Q4_K_M, and a Qwen 2.5 draft model in either 0.5B or 1.5B size. The baseline (no draft) was the fastest configuration. The 0.5B draft was 5% slower. The 1.5B draft was 10% slower. 5 trials per config, deterministic settings, 200 generated tokens per trial.

The published 1.5 to 2.0x speedup on discrete GPUs does not transfer to a single-user interactive workload on M2. The 0.5B and 1.5B draft models from the Qwen 2.5 family are cross-family relative to the Qwen 3 14B target, which gives a low acceptance rate. The draft model's overhead is not amortized enough to beat the baseline.

A Qwen 3 1.7B or 0.6B draft, if Ollama publishes one, would have a much higher acceptance rate against the Qwen 3 14B target and would likely land closer to the published speedup. Ollama v0.32.6 (August 2026) added MTP-based automatic speculative decoding that uses the model's own multi-token-prediction head, no separate draft model needed.

Docling vs Marker vs PaddleOCR (PP-OCRv6 + UVDoc) on 4 test PDFs. Marker averaged 0.86 seconds per page with 95.6% text fidelity. Docling came in at 4.80 seconds per page and is the only one that preserves borderless table structure as a real markdown table. PaddleOCR hit 26.99 seconds per page and used 4.4 GB of peak RAM.

On the table-heavy PDF, Docling scored 43.0% under the markdown-stripped edit distance metric. Marker scored 86.8% and PaddleOCR scored 85.0%. The 43% is a metric artifact, not a real failure. Docling splits each table into a header row and data rows in markdown, while the ground truth has all cells on a single line. The character-level edit distance is huge but the information is intact.

PaddleOCR's 4.4 GB peak is a real constraint on a 24 GB unified-memory machine. You can still have a browser and a code editor open while running PaddleOCR, but you cannot also load a 14B parameter LLM at the same time. Docling and Marker leave enough headroom to run a 14B Q4 model side-by-side.

Qwen3 14B picks the right tool 9 out of 10 times on the test suite. Llama 3.2 3B is 25x faster but only picks the right tool 5 out of 10 times. The trade-off is real: for a code agent that picks the wrong tool 50% of the time, the latency advantage is irrelevant.

Tool-calling benchmarks often use a synthetic test suite with JSON-mode validation. The Hard Numbers test suite used 20 real tool definitions drawn from the GitHub MCP, including Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, and WebFetch. Each model was given 10 tasks that required 1-3 tool calls to complete.

On Apple M2 with 24 GB, MLX is 1.42x faster than Ollama on chat workloads (decode-bound, single-stream). Ollama is 1.7x faster on RAG workloads (prefill-bound, batched context). The crossover is around 4K tokens of context: below 4K, MLX wins; above 4K, Ollama wins. The RAG number is dominated by Ollama's superior prompt processing throughput.

Both engines use the same Qwen3 14B Q4_K_M weights. MLX converts them to MLX format at load time, which takes about 3 seconds on M2. Ollama loads the GGUF directly. After the one-time conversion, MLX has a smaller per-token decode cost on M2 because it can take advantage of the unified memory architecture more directly.

Three Apache 2.0 open-weight 14-24B LLMs head-to-head: gpt-oss-20B (OpenAI's first open-weight model since GPT-2), Qwen3-14B, and Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501. MMLU: 71.2 / 75.8 / 76.4. HumanEval: 78.0 / 81.0 / 79.5. GSM8K: 84.5 / 89.0 / 88.0. IFEval: 82.1 / 84.3 / 80.6. Qwen3-14B wins 3 of 4, Mistral-Small wins 1 (MMLU by 0.6 points).

gpt-oss-20B uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with 20.9B total parameters but only 3.6B active per token. It is the first model from OpenAI with MXFP4 (microscaling 4-bit float) quantization as the native format. On Apple Silicon without hardware MXFP4 support, the model has to dequantize to a different format at load time, which costs some of the speed advantage.

On Apple M2 24GB, the dequantization penalty makes gpt-oss-20B run at 2.6 tok/s, which is about half the speed of the older Qwen3-14B at 4.7 tok/s. The published gpt-oss numbers on H100s show 1.7x faster than Qwen3 at the same accuracy tier, but that speedup requires MXFP4 hardware support that M2 does not have.

Tested 6 local LLMs on an Apple M2 with 24 GB of unified memory: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 14B, Mistral-Small 24B, Phi-3 Medium 14B, Gemma-2 27B, and DeepSeek-Coder-V2 16B. Memory usage ranged from 5.1 GB (Llama 3.1 8B) to 15.4 GB (Gemma-2 27B). Tokens per second ranged from 1.8 (Gemma-2 27B) to 18.4 (Llama 3.1 8B).
